t: What Velcro Cable Rolls and Cut-to-Length Straps Are
title: What Velcro Cable Rolls and Cut-to-Length Straps Are
description: Velcro cable rolls — hook-and-loop straps sold on a roll you cut to length, like VELCRO Brand ONE-WRAP — are the reusable way to bundle PC cables. You cut a strap, wrap it around the cable bundle, and press it closed; to change the bundle you just peel it open. Unlike zip ties they are infinitely reusable and never need cutting off, which makes them the default for any cable you might reroute.

demo.program:
bundle = ["24-pin ATX", "8-pin EPS", "2x PCIe 8-pin", "SATA power x3"]
straps_needed = len(bundle) + 2   # one per cable + spares
print("PSU cables to manage:", len(bundle))
print("Velcro straps to cut:", straps_needed, "(reusable: cut once, use forever)")
print("Rule: any cable you might reroute gets velcro, not zip ties.")

title: How Hook-and-Loop Holds Without Adhesive
description: Hook-and-loop fastening uses tiny hooks on one side that catch loops on the other — thousands of micro-connections per square inch that peel apart easily but resist shear. ONE-WRAP style straps have hooks on one face and loops on the other, so the strap sticks to itself with no separate piece. The hold is strong against sliding along the bundle but opens with a peel, which is exactly the behavior cable management wants.

demo.program:
print("Hooks catch loops: thousands of micro-connections per square inch.")
print("Strong in SHEAR (bundle can't slide) / easy in PEEL (opens by hand).")
print("ONE-WRAP: hooks one face, loops other -> strap sticks to ITSELF.")
print("Result: firm bundle, zero tools to open.")

t: Widths, Lengths, and Rolls: What to Buy
title: Widths, Lengths, and Rolls: What to Buy
description: The useful widths are 1/2 inch for thin bundles (fan cables, front-panel wires), 3/4 inch as the general PC size, and 1 inch for thick PSU cable groups. Rolls commonly come in 25-foot and 50-foot lengths; a 25-foot roll of 3/4-inch strap handles several full builds. Pre-cut straps exist but cost more per strap — the roll plus scissors is the economical choice.

demo.program:
widths = [("1/2 in", "fan cables, front-panel wires"),
          ("3/4 in", "general PC bundles (the default)"),
          ("1 in", "thick PSU cable groups")]
for w, use in widths:
    print(f"  {w:<8} -> {use}")
print("Buy: 25-ft roll of 3/4 in (~$10) + scissors. Handles several full builds.")

t: Cutting and Sizing Straps for Clean Bundles
title: Cutting and Sizing Straps for Clean Bundles
description: Size each strap to wrap the bundle one and a half times — one full wrap plus overlap for the hook-and-loop to bite. Too short and the strap pops open; too long and the tail sticks out and looks messy. Cut with scissors, not a knife, and round the corners slightly so they do not catch. Pre-cut a handful of common sizes before a build so strapping never interrupts the workflow.

demo.program:
import math
for dia_in, name in [(0.5, "fan bundle"), (1.0, "SATA group"), (1.5, "PSU trunk")]:
    strap = math.pi * dia_in * 1.5
    print(f"  {name:<10} dia {dia_in} in -> cut {strap:.1f} in strap")
print("Formula: strap length = pi x bundle diameter x 1.5")

title: Routing Technique: The Behind-the-Tray Run
description: The classic clean build routes PSU cables behind the motherboard tray and brings each one through the nearest grommet to its connector. Velcro straps anchor the trunk to the tray's tie points every 6 to 8 inches so the bundle lies flat and the side panel closes without pressure. Strap the trunk first, then branch individual cables — trunk-then-branch is the whole technique in three words.

demo.program:
trunk_len_in = 24
spacing = 7
n = trunk_len_in // spacing + 1
print(f"Trunk {trunk_len_in} in, strap every ~{spacing} in -> {n} straps")
print("Order: 1) lay trunk behind tray 2) strap to tie points 3) branch cables out")
print("Panel must close with ZERO pressure on the bundle.")

t: Use Case: PSU Cable Management in a Full Build
title: Use Case: PSU Cable Management in a Full Build
description: A modular PSU's cable set is the biggest bundling job in the case: 24-pin, EPS, PCIe, and SATA runs. Group by destination — motherboard power together, GPU power together, drives together — strap each group behind the tray, and leave service loops (a few inches of slack) at the PSU end so cables can be rerouted later. Velcro means the next upgrade does not start with cutting a dozen zip ties.

t: Use Case: Fan and Front-Panel Wire Bundles
title: Use Case: Fan and Front-Panel Wire Bundles
description: Fan cables and front-panel wires are thin, numerous, and ugly — the perfect velcro job. Gather each fan's cable along its frame with a 1/2-inch strap, then bundle all fan cables into one trunk running to the headers. Front-panel wires (power, reset, LEDs, USB) bundle into one flat group along the case edge. Thin bundles need short straps; a long strap on a thin bundle just makes a floppy tail.

demo.program:

print(f"{fans} fan cables: 1/2-in strap per fan frame, then one trunk to headers")
print(f"{fp_wires} front-panel wires: one flat bundle along case edge")
print("Match strap length to bundle: thin bundle + long strap = floppy tail.")

t: Use Case: Under-Desk and Behind-Monitor Cable Runs
title: Use Case: Under-Desk and Behind-Monitor Cable Runs
description: Velcro straps tame the desk too: bundle monitor power, display cables, and USB runs into one trunk along the desk edge, strap every foot, and anchor the trunk with adhesive clips. Because straps reopen, adding a new peripheral means peeling one strap, laying the cable in, and pressing closed — a thirty-second job. Desk cable management only survives if changes are this easy.

print("Add a peripheral: peel one strap, lay cable in, press closed (30 seconds).")

t: Velcro Straps vs Zip Ties: The Reusability Divide
title: Velcro Straps vs Zip Ties: The Reusability Divide
description: Velcro straps cost more per piece but are reusable hundreds of times; zip ties cost pennies but are single-use and need cutters to remove. Velcro cannot be overtightened enough to damage cables; zip ties cinched hard can deform insulation. The working rule: velcro everywhere you might ever change, zip ties only for permanent hidden runs you will never touch again.

demo.program:
print("velcro: reusable 100x+, hand-open, can't crush cables, ~$0.20/strap")
print("zip tie: single-use, needs cutters, can deform insulation, ~$0.02/tie")
print("RULE: velcro anywhere you might change; zip ties only for permanent hidden runs.")

title: Strap Maintenance and Lifespan
description: Hook-and-loop wears out: after a few hundred open-close cycles the hooks straighten and hold weakens, and lint packed into the loops kills grip long before that. Revive straps by picking lint out of the loop side with tweezers; replace straps that no longer hold a firm peel. A roll stored dry and dark lasts years — UV and heat age the hooks faster than use does.

demo.program:
print("Lifespan: hundreds of cycles; lint is the #1 killer (pick out with tweezers).")
print("Replace when: peel feels weak, bundle slides, hooks visibly straightened.")
print("Storage: dry + dark. UV and heat age hooks faster than use.")

title: Color-Coding Bundles With Colored Straps
description: Straps come in black, white, and colors — use the colors as labels: red straps on GPU power, blue on storage, yellow on fan trunks. In a dark case the color reads instantly under a headlamp, so troubleshooting means following the red bundle, not tracing cables. Black for the visible runs keeps the aesthetic clean; colors live behind the tray where they work as labels.

t: Buying Guide: Genuine vs Generic Hook-and-Loop
title: Buying Guide: Genuine vs Generic Hook-and-Loop
description: Genuine VELCRO Brand ONE-WRAP uses denser hooks and lasts noticeably longer than thin generic rolls, which fray at the cut edge and lose grip sooner. For a few builds a year, generic is fine; for a shop doing weekly builds, genuine pays for itself in not re-strapping. Check the roll's thickness — flimsy thin strap stretches and lets bundles sag. Expect 8 to 15 dollars for a 25-foot roll.

demo.program:
print("Genuine ONE-WRAP: denser hooks, longer life, ~$12-15 / 25 ft")
print("Generic: fine for a few builds/year, frays sooner, ~$8 / 25 ft")
print("Shop doing weekly builds -> genuine pays for itself in re-strap labor.")
print("Check thickness: flimsy strap stretches, bundles sag.")

t: Advanced: Strap Anchors and Tie-Point Improvisation
title: Advanced: Strap Anchors and Tie-Point Improvisation
description: Cases have built-in tie points, but desks and test benches do not — improvise anchors with adhesive cable mounts: stick a mount, loop a strap through it, and the strap becomes a fixed anchor point. On open test benches, anchor PSU cable trunks to the bench edge so cables cannot drag the board. A strap through an anchor beats a strap around nothing every time.

demo.program:
print("No tie points? adhesive mount + strap through it = instant anchor.")
print("Test bench: anchor PSU trunks to bench edge (cables can't drag the board).")
print("A strap through an anchor beats a strap around nothing.")

t: Pro Technique: The Service Loop and Future-Proof Bundle
title: Pro Technique: The Service Loop and Future-Proof Bundle
description: Every trunk gets a service loop — 3 to 4 inches of extra cable folded and strapped at the PSU or source end. When a GPU upgrade needs a longer PCIe run or a drive moves bays, the loop pays out instead of forcing a re-route. Strap the loop flat against the trunk so it looks intentional. Future-proofing is just slack, strapped neatly, in the right place.

demo.program:
print("Service loop: 3-4 in extra cable, folded + strapped at the source end.")
print("GPU upgrade / drive move: loop pays out, no re-route needed.")
print("Strap the loop flat to the trunk: slack looks intentional, not messy.")
